You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failing test `testWriteNonAsciiDirectoryNamePosixMode` in `TarArchiveOutputStreamTest` is trying to add a directory with a name longer than 100 bytes to a TAR Archive. This operation generates an exception due to the request to write more bytes than the size in the header for the entry. The exception indicates that the size in the header is '0' bytes, causing an `IOException`.

Looking at the test snippet, it attempts to create a `TarArchiveEntry` for a directory with the name "f\u00f6\u00f6/". This directory name contains non-ASCII characters, which may contribute to the issue of exceeding the size limit in the TAR Archive header.

The current bug report describes the specific problem of long directory names not being stored in the TAR Archive due to errors when writing PAX headers. This aligns with the observed behavior in the failing test.

Based on the failure and the bug report, it seems that a directory name with non-ASCII characters is causing the TAR Archive to exceed the size limit specified in the header, leading to an `IOException` during the operation of adding the entry to the TAR Archive.

This issue may be related to how the length of the directory name is handled or encoded in the TAR Archive creation process.

Now, I will inspect the relevant code snippet to further investigate the root cause.

The `TarArchiveOutputStream` constructor that takes an `OutputStream` as a parameter initializes the object with default block size and record size values.

To locate the specific logic related to adding entries to the TAR Archive and handling directory names, we should look into the methods responsible for adding entries and managing the header information in the `TarArchiveOutputStream` class, such as the method that sets entries, manages headers, or handles non-ASCII characters in directory names.

messages.content:
The issue is likely originating in the `writePaxHeaders` method of the `TarArchiveOutputStream` class. This method is responsible for writing PAX headers for extended attributes, which may include handling long directory names.

The `writePaxHeaders` method constructs PAX extended headers for the entry name in the TAR Archive. If the name is longer than a certain length, it may be truncated in the process of creating the header, potentially leading to the size mismatch issue mentioned in the bug report.

To resolve the problem of long directory names not being stored in the TAR Archive properly, you should investigate the logic in the `writePaxHeaders` method that calculates the header length and adjusts the name if it exceeds the maximum length allowed.

Here are the methods that would be the best locations to fix the issue:
- `org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.tar.TarArchiveOutputStream.writePaxHeaders(java.lang.String, java.util.Map<java.lang.String, java.lang.String>)`

These methods are likely where adjustments can be made to handle long directory names correctly in the TAR Archive creation process.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
